canberra.title: Public outcry triggers review of ACT sexual violence sentencing laws
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. The laws that direct courts to consider an offender’s age when sentencing ...
canberra.content:
An ACT Government review will examine sentencing laws – but only in relation to sexually violent offences. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

The laws that direct courts to consider an offender’s age when sentencing them – and taking prison off the table unless there are no other options – will be central to a review of Canberra’s sentencing legislation for sexually violent crimes.

The sentencing of a teenager who raped a young woman near a house party (referred to as the Hancock case) has led to public outcry about the factors that are considered by the courts when handing down punishments.

Shadow Attorney-General Chiaka Barry brought a motion to the Legislative Assembly on Tuesday (20 October) calling for an inquiry into the ACT’s sentencing practices for sexually violent crimes and for the new powers to allow the Attorney-General to direct the Director of Public Prosecutions to appeal a court’s sentence if it is seen to be “manifestly inadequate” and in the public interest.

“Canberrans are telling us that their confidence in the justice system – and the justice system as a whole – has been shaken,” she said.

“They are asking whether the system is delivering justice, whether victims are being heard and whether the balance between the rights of the offending and the safety of the community is right.”

Ms Barry said her motion wasn’t about the Hancock case itself, but the remarks of the sentencing justice served as a “catalyst” for the reason why a major review was needed now.

She said there were some areas of the system where politicians “must keep our hands to ourselves”, but laws also cannot be “set and forget”.

“The uncomfortable truth is that the decisions and policies of this government, in the context of sentencing, must be scrutinised,” Ms Barry said.

“A review alone is not enough – and I admit that. But it shows a good start at a solid basis for reform.

“More importantly, the review must lead to action.”

Attorney-General Tara Cheyne moved amendments which removed any consideration of giving her position more power to direct the DPP.

But she said a targeted review of sentencing laws was appropriate.

“A lack of sexual experience or a lack of familiarity with Australian societal norms is not an excuse for sexual violence,” Ms Cheyne said.

“Consent is not optional.

“But there is a distinction between the law that applies to everyone, and the factors that a court is permitted to weigh when it sentences [an individual].”

Her amendments called for a targeted review of the ACT’s sentencing laws specifically in relation to sexual violence.

In particular, it would look at implementation of recommendations from the 2021 Listen. Take Action to Prevent, Believe and Heal report, suspended sentences, mitigating factors that can be considered during sentencing, community safety measures for punishments served outside of prison, and the provisions for young offenders.

The latter has not been examined since they were added to the law in 2008.

“It is the young offender provisions in particular which I feel have been somewhat lost in the public discourse – the provisions which require a court to treat imprisonment of a young person as a last resort [and, if applied] for the shortest appropriate term,” Ms Cheyne said.

“Almost 20 years [since the young offenders provisions were included], there is a question of whether, for the most serious sexual offences, that remains the right instruction.”

When finishing her debate, Ms Cheyne had this message for victim-survivors of sexual violence: “You deserve to be heard. You deserve to be treated with dignity, and you deserve a justice system worthy of your trust.

“I cannot change what happened to this young woman … but we can and we will examine whether our laws are working as they should, identify where they need to change, and take responsibility for changing them, with the voices of victim-survivors in the room.”

Ms Barry expressed her disappointment that the additional powers section of her motion was removed.

She also wasn’t impressed that the amendments removed requirements for the review to examine broader ACT sentencing law for all offences, and how they are leading to better outcomes across all crime types.

“This was an opportunity to identify for the community that rehabilitation leads to a better outcome [in the ACT],” Ms Barry said.

“Sadly, it’s going to be missed.”

The amended motion was passed with the support of ACT Labor, ACT Greens and independent MLAs.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Accused kidnapper allegedly posted videos of brutal assaults to social media
canberra.snippet: An alleged kidnapper from Canberra filmed himself brutally assaulting a man before posting the videos to social media, a court has heard....
canberra.content:
20 October 2026

A 27-year-old man has been charged with kidnapping after he allegedly posted videos to social media showing him assaulting his victim. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

An alleged kidnapper from Canberra filmed himself brutally assaulting a man before posting the videos to social media, a court has heard.

It was not immediately clear how the 27-year-old defendant knew his alleged victim, but an ACT Policing spokesperson said the latter had gone over to the former’s home in Dunlop, Canberra on Saturday (10 October).

The spokesperson alleged the defendant then became violent and demanded the man give him back cash that he claimed had been stolen from him.

The defendant allegedly stopped the man from leaving, then repeatedly assaulted him the following day. As a result, the alleged victim was left with cuts, facial fractures and bruising from being hit with a weapon.

It is also alleged the defendant forced the man to drink a liquid that affected his consciousness.

Late on Sunday evening (11 October), the defendant put the man into a car and drove him to Queanbeyan, NSW.

The police spokesperson alleged he continued to assault the man while recording the abuse on his phone.

The defendant allegedly took the man back to ACT on Monday (12 October). The man regained consciousness in parkland near Lance Hill Avenue in Dunlop before seeking help at a nearby home.

“The victim was transported to hospital where he was treated for multiple injuries,” the police spokesperson said.

“He has since been discharged.”

The defendant was arrested and charged with a kidnapping offence before he faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Tuesday (20 October).

Special Magistrate Michael Cowen said the allegations detailed “a prolonged period of violence” against a person the defendant knew.

He also said it was alleged the defendant uploaded videos of himself assaulting the man to the social media apps Instagram and Snapchat.

The defendant’s lawyer, Eimear Silk of Legal Aid, said health professionals had recommended her client be taken to hospital for a mental health assessment.

But prosecutor Sam McLaughlin said he was concerned about this approach, as when being assessed by a health professional, the defendant had reportedly expressed “violent ideation and plans to harm others around him”.

Mr McLaughlin said he was concerned about the welfare of others at the mental health unit if the defendant was taken there.

Ms Silk said her client could be held at the Dhulwa Mental Health Unit rather than in Canberra Hospital, as it was a secure facility.

Special Magistrate Cowen ultimately said he was satisfied he should order the defendant be taken for a mental health assessment.

The court did not hear which facility the defendant will be taken to, but he will return to court in the future to be formally charged. He has not been named while the assessment takes place.

canberra.title: Haines has lost one leg and doctors fighting to save the other
canberra.snippet: Independent member for Indi, Helen Haines, has lost one leg, and doctors are trying to save the other, following Monday’s horrific vehicl...
canberra.content:
Federal MP Helen Haines has lost one leg and is fighting for her life in Melbourne’s Alfred Hospital. Photo: Helen Haines.

Independent member for Indi, Helen Haines, has lost one leg, and doctors are trying to save the other, following Monday’s horrific vehicle attack on the much-loved MP.

She remains in a critical condition in Melbourne’s Alfred Hospital, where she was medevacced after being deliberately rammed twice while standing in a carpark near her Wangaratta electorate office.

Praise has poured out for Dr Haines from across the local and wider Australian community, as well as from across the political divide.

Addressing an audience in Melbourne, Anthony Albanese continued to give high praise to the independent MP who is now fighting for her life.

“Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives,” the Prime Minister said.

“Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed, strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.

“I was asked earlier today when someone suggested ‘could we do a vigil somewhere? What can we do to show our support and solidarity between fellows at this difficult time?’

“My response to them, when I thought about it, was just ‘be like Helen: kindness, compassion, caring’.”

One privately organised vigil being mooted by some campaigners close to Dr Haines encourages people to put two chairs on their front lawns to honour her habit of placing an orange chair outside to invite people in for a conversation.

The Prime Minister, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke and Victorian Premier Ben Carroll all met with AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett and Victorian Police Commissioner Mike Bush in Melbourne on Tuesday to be briefed on the investigation.

The alleged attacker has been named as 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, who is reported to be a long-term anti-forestry campaigner.

The PM also publicly praised local barber Rick Jefferies, who stepped in to restrain Nugent during the attack.

Mr Jefferies made a dramatic citizen’s arrest, but has downplayed any notion of himself being a hero.

“This is just a bloke,” Mr Albanese said.

“He said it was just the right thing to do, but he did run into danger, not knowing what the consequences could potentially be for him.

“Just running to help someone else. A great example of the Australian spirit and the best of the Australian character.

“So I think that even in dark times we see light. What Ricky represents is light, and light will win over darkness each and every time.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said his “thoughts and prayers” were also with Dr Haines and her family.

“This is a country where we resolve our differences through vigorous debate, through choice at the ballot box, but not through violence in any way, shape, or form,” he said.

“We must all absolutely condemn crossing that line.

“I think one of the reasons we’ve been so successful as a country is that we’ve understood that line.

“We’ve understood that Australians love a good debate, we’re up-front people and that’s great, there’s no problem with that at all.

“But what we should never, ever do is allow that to cross the line into any form of violence, and what we saw yesterday was un-Australian and unacceptable and must be condemned by absolutely all of us and, as I say, our thoughts and prayers are with Helen and her family at this time.”

Greens leader David Shoebridge described Dr Haines as his friend and said he was holding on to hope for her recovery and some good news.

“Helen is one of the most extraordinary people in parliament. She is a strong voice for her community, a leading voice against corruption, and a powerful voice for compassion and humanity in parliament,” Senator Shoebridge said.

“In parliament, as in person, Helen is generous with her time and attention and is always willing to help others. I have had the benefit of her generosity.

“The notion she could be targeted for her work is horrifying, senseless and shameful.”

canberra.title: Armed guards contracted to keep Legislative Assembly safe
canberra.snippet: Armed security guards have been contracted to patrol the Legislative Assembly for the first time to keep MLAs and staff safe, Speaker Jer...
canberra.content:
Speaker Jeremy Hanson says the risk to MLAs has increased markedly in the past few years. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Armed security guards have been contracted to patrol the Legislative Assembly for the first time to keep MLAs and staff safe, Speaker Jeremy Hanson has revealed in the wake of the attack on Indi MP Helen Haines.

The Speaker outlined the Assembly security response after the Chief Minister and Opposition Leader expressed support for Dr Haines and said they had both been the target of increasingly nasty online attacks.

Mr Hanson said it was a sad state of affairs, but the contract and upgrades to the Legislative Assembly building entrance were necessary because ASIO and the Australian Federal Police had increasingly serious threat assessments about the nation’s political representatives.

He said that over the past few years there had been a definite increase in risk to MLAs.

“That, from my view, comes from two major areas,” Mr Hanson told Region.

“One is the politically motivated violence, and certainly we’ve received briefings from ASIO, and you can turn to the Director-General’s comments and threat assessments, and then there are these fixated individuals, and we get advice from the Australian Federal Police.

“But regardless of where that threat emanates and why, at the end of the day, when it comes to the Assembly, we need to be capable of responding to an armed intruder.”

Mr Hanson said a security review of the Assembly was conducted last year, the front entrance had been changed, and physical security measures there boosted.

The budget also funded other security upgrades, including security cameras and access points, and a contract for armed security guards.

Mr Hanson said ASIO Director General Mike Burgess had made the point in 2025 that politically motivated violence was already flashing red and was expected to remain elevated.

“In his 2026 threat assessment, he said politically motivated violence, which incorporates terrorism, remains an acute concern, and I’m gravely concerned by its temperature and trajectory,” he said.

Members themselves had reported an increasingly dangerous environment.

Mr Hanson said a members survey had identified an increase in the volume and the nature of threats online and direct, including threats of sexual violence and death.

He did not identify any particular incident, and there was no specified threat to the Assembly at present, but the aim was to take preventative measures.

“This is in response to the environment in which we find ourselves,” Mr Hanson said.

“I want to make sure that we are prepared for those contingencies, and if something does happen, we need to have the physical security in place, but also have the people that can respond, have the right training, the right equipment and can respond immediately if there is a threat.”

Police Minister Marisa Paterson had organised a briefing with police for all members and senior staff, and these would be ongoing. Members also recently received a briefing from ASIO.

“The conversation is ongoing, and we’ve got to make sure that we are keeping abreast of any particular threats.”

Mr Hanson said all MLAs wanted to retain the ACT’s open democracy and remain available to the public in both the Assembly and the community.

“It’s a balancing act, but ultimately these are security measures that I have considered are necessary,” he said.

“I’ve received support from the government for these measures. It is a sad state of affairs, but it is the reality in the environment in which we find ourselves.”

Mr Hanson said MLAs were mindful of what they said or posted, and he was proud of how the Assembly conducted itself.

“The debate can from time to time become robust as it should, but I think it is by and large civil and respectful,” he said.

Mr Hanson said incidents like the attack on Dr Haines could not be allowed to assault democracy.

“Our thoughts are very much with Dr Haines and her friends and family,” he said. “It’s a very sad situation we find ourselves in, but we’ve got to make sure that democracy thrives. We must stand up to this sort of thing.”

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the Chief Police Officer, Deputy Commissioner Scott Lee, had spoken with Dr Paterson about the safety of MLAs and staff.

ACT Policing had established arrangements for MLAs and their offices to report any issues or matters of concern to police.

This included matters referred to the ACT Policing Fixated Threat Assessment Centre, where reports were assessed so that an appropriate police response and, where needed, broader government support services could be provided.

ACT Policing confirmed that MLAs would receive a security briefing this week on the current security environment.

“ACT Policing continues to monitor this increasingly complex security environment while working with our partners and the community to support public safety and confidence,” the spokesperson said.

Mr Barr said that in the current environment the attack on Dr Haines was not surprising.

He said the risk threat to politicians had become more heightened in recent years.

“It does feel elevated, greater in volume, sharper and meaner, frankly, in tone,” he told ABC radio.

“I’ve copped homophobic abuse throughout my career, but it’s going beyond that now too.”

Mr Parton echoed the Prime Minister’s pleas to turn the temperature down.

In a social media post, he said that for most of his time in politics, no one had said they wanted to harm him in any way, but “in the last two or three years, wow, it’s just been crazy”.

Later, he said discussion on social media and in direct messages had absolutely ramped up, and not in a good way.

Mr Parton said the social media algorithm, which favoured conflict and anger, was partly to blame.

“We need to all take stock and understand that there are many more things that unite us than divide us and be kind and just be sensible Australians,” he said.

canberra.title: Teen admits plotting white supremacist terrorist attack in Canberra
canberra.snippet: A young man has admitted he was arrested while plotting to conduct a white supremacy-inspired terrorist attack in Canberra that would hav...
canberra.content:
20 October 2026

An 18-year-old man has pleaded guilty to two terrorism-related charges in the ACT Supreme Court. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A young man has admitted he was arrested while plotting to conduct a white supremacy-inspired terrorist attack in Canberra that would have resulted in injuries or death.

This means the now-18-year-old will become the first person in the ACT to be sentenced for planning to commit a terrorist act.

He was 17 when he was arrested in November 2025, which means he legally cannot be named due to his age.

A police raid on his bedroom allegedly found some of the materials needed to make chlorine gas, as well as gas masks, military-style clothing and texts relating to Nazism.

He was refused bail while his charges progressed through the courts. He had been scheduled to face a three-week trial in the ACT Supreme Court next month.

But instead, he faced the Supreme Court again this week and pleaded guilty to two counts of committing acts in preparation of a terrorist act.

The court heard that through his pleas, he admitted collecting gas masks, chemicals, documents and equipment related to making gases which could be used in an act of terrorism and would have caused death or serious harm.

He also admitted acting this way to advance white supremacy and wanted to intimidate a government or the public with his behaviour.

His other charges will be dropped.

While the teen pleaded guilty to the two charges, the court heard lawyers had not yet reached agreement on a document that outlined the details of his offences.

The matter was adjourned to November so the parties could agree on the document and the court could set a sentencing date.

The court heard sentencing will likely take place in the first half of 2027.

The teen, who remains in custody, gave a brief smile and nod to his parents in the courtroom gallery before guards led him out of the room.

The charge of acts in preparation, or planning for, a terrorist act carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

australia.title: A chaotic few minutes and a beloved MP’s life in the balance: a community grapples with the unfathomable
australia.snippet: Wangaratta locals who went to Helen Haines’ aid on Monday have been hailed as heroes. But many remain shellshocked by the alleged attack ...
australia.content:
It sounded like a car accident – as though someone had unintentionally backed into another vehicle on the quiet main street in the north-east Victorian city of Wangaratta.

Across the road, Cody Lepoidevin had been helping a customer in the High Country RoadHouse – an outdoor store directly across from the office of his local federal MP, Helen Haines.

It was about 3.35pm on Monday. Haines had finished her drive back to the office from a sod-turning event in Mansfield – passing state forests and farmland that make up much of the scenery of the region along the way. As Haines stood at the back of her car, a white Toyota did a U-turn in the street and allegedly rammed into her.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged over what Victoria police allege was a targeted attack.

Lepoidevin’s boss, Jason Bacon, says people ran out of the store, expecting to see two cars crash into each other. He says Lepoidevin watched the driver allegedly reverse and hit Haines again.

“Cody, one of the young guys at work, actually initially saw the impact and actually ran over there to help,” Bacon says.

“He heard a car run up the back of another car over there and he walked out, instinctively, thinking it was a car accident.”

Once passersby realised what was happening, Bacon says, “they sprang into action”.

Lepoidevin told his boss about hearing Haines crying out, and how he and two or three customers rushed across the road to help.

Meanwhile, a local barber had just finished with a family who came in for haircuts when he heard the crash just outside the shop.

“A lot of people, a lot of people got involved immediately, and they didn’t even check the danger,” Ricky Jefferies says.

“They just ran to help. The driver was still in the car, the car was still on.

“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do.”

The next few minutes were chaos. One person jumped in front of the Toyota, while Jefferies ran to the car to get the driver out.

He pulled him from his seat, before wrestling him to the ground, Jefferies says. He says he told the man he couldn’t leave, but tried to calm him while others helped Haines. He also alleges the man had a knife on him, which was thrown away.

Haines was on the bitumen, having suffered serious injuries to both her legs. Haines has had one leg amputated.

Jefferies – and the others who rushed to her aid – have been hailed as heroes by Australia’s political leader. The driver has been in custody since.

‘Helen is not a person that just would have any enemies’

Bacon arrived at his store 30 minutes after the alleged attack to find customers still hiding at the back.

“Everyone ran when it happened. There were a few people helping out, and those that couldn’t directly help were pretty impacted by it,” he says.

“We closed the door and had some customers in here for about an hour after.”

On Tuesday, Wangaratta remains in shock. The main street is quiet, aside from a large media throng outside Haines’ office. The front door is slowly being obscured by cards and flowers, as community members leave messages hoping for a quick recovery.

On the streets, locals reflect the mood. They’re a tight-knit community where nothing like this happens. The shock is palpable. For the quiet regional city, it’s hard to comprehend.

Matthew Bolton is walking past her office as people lay flowers. He says it is hard to fathom what happened. “It’s surreal that something like this has happened in Wangaratta, of all places,” he says.

“She means so much to the community. She’s done so much over a long period of time without asking much in return.”

Louise Middleton, dressed in a bright orange “Helen Haines for Indi” T-shirt, comes to lay flowers. She had volunteered for Haines in the last two elections.

“My husband said Helen had been hit by a car and I just thought … I was just hoping it was a minor thing. But then as it all sort of unfolded … it’s just mind-boggling,” Middleton says.

“Helen is not a person that just would have any enemies. She’s not a very divisive character and pretty much everyone loves her. So it’s really confusing.”

A bit down the street, Chris Wernert talks of how he couldn’t sleep on Monday night. So he got up, found an old T-shirt and wrote on it: “Wangaratta this is not us.” Wernert was down waving the Australian flag outside Haines’ office after the incident on Tuesday.

“I saw a guy walking up the street last night,” he says. “This guy in his 60s, carrying an envelope and flowers that he dropped off. There were tears in his eyes.”

Like many in the community, he says he respects Haines. If you don’t share her views, she will still come and talk to you, Wernert says. She is always respectful, always willing to hear a different option.

“We want people to be able to talk to each other,” he says. “Some of their views might be a bit hard to take on board and listen to. But we’ve got to have that. Otherwise we get garbage like this. We don’t want this in Australia. We do not want this.”

australia.title: Helen Haines loses leg as surgeons fight to save the other after alleged attack in Wangaratta
australia.snippet: Independent MP is in critical yet stable condition after man allegedly did U-turn to strike her twice with his car Brendan Nugent’s famil...
australia.content:
The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office, causing her to lose one of her legs.

The member for Indi was airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.

Surgeons were on Tuesday fighting to save Haines’ other leg, as the 65-year-old remained in a critical condition.

A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene. The alleged attacker is Brendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.

Nugent was charged on Tuesday night with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the Commonwealth offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Victoria police confirmed in a statement that they would allege the attack was targeted. Nugent is expected to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday.

Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and Rod’s partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement that Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years.

“What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” they said.

“We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.”

Anthony Albanese confirmed authorities believed the attack was deliberate.

“Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives,” the prime minister said on Tuesday afternoon.

“Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed to strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.”

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said witnesses alleged the driver completed a U-turn before the incident.

“What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time,” he told ABC radio.

“A bystander ran towards the scene, got the driver out of the vehicle and held the driver until police arrived.”

Ricky Jefferies, whose barbershop is next door to Haines’ office, ran from his shop to help after hearing the crash.

“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,” he told reporters on Tuesday morning.

Jefferies, who returned to work on Tuesday morning, alleged the driver had a knife on him. “He didn’t pull it out,” he said. “Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away.”

Burke said: “I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place.”

The home affairs minister said the nation’s security agencies and police would be working through what more could have been done to prevent the alleged attack and to help keep others safe.

On Monday, Burke reported that there had been 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, an increase from 951 the year before.

“We already knew that we needed to do more to be able to keep people in public office safe and we have been,” he said.

“While we don’t make public the dollar figures and the exact provision of security for obvious reasons … we had a very significant uplift in the budget.

“There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action.”

Albanese has been joined by leaders and parliamentarians from across the country in calling for a calming of political discourse.

The mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, expressed gratitude to Jefferies for stepping in to stop the man.

“I spoke to the barber this morning and he just shrugged his shoulders. He seemed to just take it in his stride. This was something that he had to do and he did it,” she said.

“He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.”

Wangaratta, the rural city in which the incident occurred, is a tightknit community in north-east Victoria. At the last census it had a population of about 20,000 people, while the broader local government area had just under 30,000.

Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been key to the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission, as well as campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access and pushing back on misuse of taxpayer funds, or pork barrelling.

australia.title: Brendan Nugent’s family say Helen Haines has been their friend for more than 20 years
australia.snippet: Father of 43-year-old Tarrawingee man who allegedly attacked the independent MP says incident is ‘devastating and unfathomable’ Who is He...
australia.content:
The father of a 43-year-old man accused of allegedly attacking Helen Haines has pledged to work with police and described the incident as “shocking and horrific”.

The independent MP remained in a critical condition on Tuesday after being airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night. She has lost one leg, with surgeons working to save the other.

Police confirmed a 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene.

Brendan Nugent was charged on Tuesday night with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the Commonwealth offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Victoria police confirmed in a statement that they would allege the attack was targeted. Nugent is expected to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday.

In a statement, Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and Rod’s partner, Christine Cunningham, said Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years.

“What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” they said.

“We would like to sincerely thank members of the local community and police who came to Helen’s aid yesterday … We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.

“Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community.”

‘Completely shocking’

Guardian Australia has spoken to local residents who have been concerned about Nugent’s behaviour for several years, including multiple allegations of abuse and threats from him.

They reported erratic behaviour, shouting and music playing loudly until the early hours of the morning. They also raised concerns about his mental health.

Nugent is a long-term forestry campaigner in the state’s north-east. Environment campaigners who worked with Nugent several years ago have expressed shock at his arrest.

Nugent has a master’s of forest ecosystems science from the University of Melbourne and spent years researching the forestry industry in Victoria. He has also been a registered business owner in Wangaratta.

Nugent was a committee member for the Save our Strathbogie Forest group, which campaigns against logging in the region. He became inactive around 2019-20.

His arrest has shocked the group’s chair, Bertrant Lobert, who said he initially appeared to be “a reasonable and thoughtful person but then he drifted away”.

“He was engaging, he was thoughtful and to hear what has happened now, if it all turns out to be true, is just completely shocking,” Lobert said.

“This is quite personal as a lot of people in our group knew Helen personally and were friends.

“This is more than just a tragedy about the targeting of public figures, it’s about our community and the people we know.”

Helen McKernan, the president of the Strathbogie Ranges Conservation Management Network Inc, also worked with Nugent as an activist before 2020.

She says Nugent lost contact with her network of forestry campaigners around this date.

“He was a committed activist,” McKernan said. “He would sleep out if necessary and help behind the scenes. We could always rely on him to turn up and contribute.”

“It’s just a shock.”

When the then-Victorian minister for environment, Lily D’Ambrosio, visited the Strathbogie forest in November 2019 to announce a ban on native forest logging, Nugent was among a group of about a dozen environmentalists who posed for photos.

Also among the group was Rebecca Swift, a friend of Dezi Freeman who owned the property where he was living when two police officers were killed and a third injured in a shooting last year.

Swift and Freeman shared conspiratorial beliefs about government and the Covid-19 pandemic, but it is unclear whether Nugent also embraced those views.

“Lily I was so pleased to be in the Strathbogie forest to hear your announcement today,” Swift commented on D’Ambrosio’s Facebook post announcing the logging ban.

“You gave us heart and hope that we are heard, and that our beloved wild landscapes are valued for so much more than merely dollars. Forest and wildlife defenders welcome a future where we can assist genuine governments to care for our national parks.”

Swift was contacted for comment.

The Victorian Nationals MP Tim McCurdy said Nugent was known to his Wangaratta office and regularly came in to raise different issues.

“He’s been at our office,” McCurdy said. “We get plenty of people come in, half a dozen a day come for various things. So yes, he’s been into our office, [to raise] various issues.

“Our office didn’t feel threatened by him, if they had they would ring the police. I want to wish Helen all the best.”

In October 2019, when Nugent was still actively campaigning on forestry issues, he praised Haines for her stance on climate change.

When Haines posted on X about an ABC Q+A episode, Nugent wrote “Would’ve been nice to include a politician who takes climate change seriously, such as yourself”.

– with AAP

australia.title: Brendan Nugent facing three charges over alleged attack on MP Helen Haines
australia.snippet: Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after the incident in Wangaratta Who is Helen Haines, the MP...
australia.content:
Helen Haines’ alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.

He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday, Victoria police confirmed in a statement, adding that it would be alleged the attack was targeted.

Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after he allegedly struck the independent MP for Indi with a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in northern Victoria.

Haines remains in a critical but stable condition after being airlifted to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery. She has lost one leg and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg.

Police also said in the statement released late on Tuesday that one of its highway patrol officers responded to the incident only eight seconds after emergency services were called.

They confirmed that a search warrant had been executed that morning at Nugent’s Great Alpine Road property.

“Victoria Police will continue to maintain an enhanced presence in Wangaratta, including members from the Public Order Response Team who have deployed to the area.

“At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter.”

australia.title: Human rights commission says ‘violence has no place in our society’ after alleged attack – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after Helen Haines critically injured Helen Haines, the pri...
australia.content:
Haines loses leg in alleged attack

The independent member for Indi has lost her leg and remains in a critical condition after being rammed by a vehicle, in what has been labelled an allegedly targeted attack.

Haines was allegedly hit by a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northern Victoria, at about 3.35pm on Monday afternoon.

She was airlifted to a Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and is fighting for her life after undergoing surgery overnight, with sources confirming to AAP the MP had lost one of her legs.

- AAP

    Barber who stopped alleged attacker speaks from Wangaratta

    What we know so far

    Haines in critical but stable condition after being rammed twice in alleged attack: Burke

    Helen Haines still in critical condition: Albanese

    Anthony Albanese: 'This is a tragic situation'

  • 17h ago

    Welcome

Summary of today's coverage, Tuesday 20 October

We’re wrapping up our live coverage of the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines.

Here’s how the day unfolded:

  • Helen Haines was critically injured in an alleged attack outside her Wangaratta electorate office in regional Victoria on Monday afternoon.

  • Haines remains in a critical condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital, where she underwent surgery overnight. The independent MP has lost one of her legs, with surgeons on Tuesday working to save her other leg.

  • Politicians from across the political spectrum have expressed their support for Haines, her family and local community. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, described her as “kind, compassionate, a person of integrity”.

  • State and local representatives across the Indi electorate released a statement calling Haines “the best of public service”.

  • Many have also expressed their concern about the rise of online hate, and violent and threatening rhetoric. New Zealand’s prime minister, Christopher Luxon, described the incident as a “terrible set of circumstances” and “a concerning development in Australia, for sure”.

  • The alleged attacker, now in custody, has been named as 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, a long-term forestry campaigner in the state’s north east. Environment campaigners who worked with Nugent several years ago have expressed shock at his arrest.

  • A major investigation is under way, with Victoria police and the Australian federal police working to identify potential charges.

Katy Gallagher condemns ‘devastating’ alleged attack

Speaking on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program, the federal finance minister said:

The idea that [an] MP had been hurt outside their electorate office doing their work, [and] that it was Helen Haynes, was just horrific.

Devastating, I think is the word I would use, and I think that’s being felt right across the political spectrum and across her electorate and across Australia.

It’s hard to get your head around, that life can change like that in a moment, for Helen. And to be critically injured and to be going through what she and her family are going through today as a consequence of her work, and her job standing up for her electorate, is just absolutely devastating.

Tess Ikonomou

Surgeons working to save Haines’ other leg

The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office, causing her to lose one of her legs.

The member for Indi was airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.

Surgeons were on Tuesday fighting to save Haines’ other leg, as the 65-year-old remained in a critical condition.

Read more:

How the events allegedly unfolded yesterday

The alleged attack on Helen Haines on Monday took place outside her Wangaratta electorate office.

The incident happened about 3.35pm and involved a four-wheel drive, which allegedly U-turned before striking Haines. The independent federal MP is in a critical but stable condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and has lost one of her legs.

A 43-year-old man has been taken to Wangaratta police station for questioning.

This map shows how the events allegedly unfolded.

‘Violence has no place,’ says human rights commission

The Australian Human Rights Commission has expressed shock and sadness at the attack on Helen Haines. In a post to social media, the commission said:

Everyone should be safe at work and in life. Violence has no place in our society.

Everyone should be treated with respect, irrespective of their political opinions, gender, faith, race or background.

Parliamentarians must be able to carry out their duties safely. This attack happened against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians. We must address intimidation, hatred, threats and violence that undermine our democracy and democratic institutions.

Zoe Daniel: ‘It was obvious … someone would get physically hurt’

The three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for Goldstein, has written a comment piece after the alleged attack.

It was obvious to those of us who work in and around politics, that eventually, someone would get physically hurt.

The fact that it’s Helen Haines, arguably the best of all of us, not just as a politician but a person, is unbearable.

Some of us community indies have T-shirts that say, “What would Helen do?”

They were a gift from the member for Kooyong, Dr Monique Ryan, a few years ago.

And while it was a bit funny at the time, it’s not a joke.

Helen is the one you go to when you’re grappling with the moral quandaries that arise frequently as an MP, in a job when a binary yes/no vote sometimes feels impossible. With intelligence, warmth and deeply held ethics, she represents the very backbone of the parliament.

Read more:

Krishani Dhanji

‘Don’t send that nasty comment’: Hastie joins calls to turn the temperature down

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he’s shocked and saddened by the alleged attack on Helen Haines, and also had concerns about his own safety and of others in Parliament.

“It’s always in the back of my mind”, he said, “which is why I stay fit and I take precautions”. Hastie was recently given extra security by the government due to threats on himself and his family, and says more broadly that the temperature needs to be turned down, particularly on social media.

Speaking to ABC radio this morning, Hastie said:

Be a better steward of Australian democracy. The worst thing we can do right now is point fingers at our political opponents and say, see, it was something that they posted or something that they said. How can we each be better? Maybe don’t like that nasty post or don’t send that nasty comment or don’t trash someone when you don’t even know who they are.

Despite their political differences, he said he held Haines in “very high regard” and called her one of the gentlest and friendliest MPs. It echoed the tributes from other politicians across federal and state parliaments who described her as “the best of us”.

Tom McIlroy

Albanese praises Haines, as MP remains in critical condition

Anthony Albanese is speaking at an event organised by The Age in Melbourne. He says Helen Haines is still in a critical condition in the Alfred Hospital.

Albanese said:

Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives.

Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed, strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.

I was asked earlier today when someone suggested ‘could we do a vigil somewhere? What can we do to show our support and solidarity between fellows at this difficult time?’

My response to them, when I thought about it, was just ‘be like Helen: kindness, compassion, caring.’

Tom McIlroy

Light will win over darkness: PM reiterates praise for barber who rushed to help

Prime minister Anthony Albanese is speaking in Melbourne and has again praised Rick Jefferies, the local barber who stepped in during the alleged attack against MP Helen Haines.

He says Jefferies’ actions represented the best of the Australian character.

“This is just a bloke,” Albanese said.

He said it was just the right thing to do, but he did run into danger, not knowing what the consequences could potentially be for him.

Just running to help someone else. A great example of the Australian spirit and the best of the Australian character.

So I think that even in dark times we see light. What Ricky represents is light, and light will be over darkness each and every time.

Haines loses leg in alleged attack

The independent member for Indi has lost her leg and remains in a critical condition after being rammed by a vehicle, in what has been labelled an allegedly targeted attack.

Haines was allegedly hit by a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northern Victoria, at about 3.35pm on Monday afternoon.

She was airlifted to a Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and is fighting for her life after undergoing surgery overnight, with sources confirming to AAP the MP had lost one of her legs.

- AAP

world.title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
world.snippet: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigrat...
world.content:
More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.

Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.

The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.

It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.

“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

world.title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors A Kenyan court ...
world.content:
A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.

Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.

Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.

He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.

Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.

Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.

Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.

People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.

Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

world.title: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
world.snippet: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war A drone strike near a market in s...
world.content:
A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.

Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.

Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.

The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”

Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.

The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.

The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.

Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.

After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.

The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.

Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.

She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”

AFP contributed to this report

world.title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
world.snippet: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO An eighth person in Kenya has teste...
world.content:
An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.

It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.

The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.

“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.

In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.

Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.

“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”

The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.

“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.

The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.

“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”

The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”

Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.

The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.

A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.

Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of ‌infections in the country was eight.

Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.

“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.

A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.

In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.

Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.

Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.

“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.

Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.

Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

world.title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
world.snippet: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds For the 2015 fresh...
world.content:
For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.

Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.

These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.

Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.

The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.

A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.

Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.

Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.

Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.

Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.

“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”
